units.title: He is God, One
units.meaning: Four short lines, and the whole of Islamic theology is in them. God is one — not first among several, not one part of something larger. The second line gives Him a name that has no clean English equivalent: the one everything depends on and who depends on nothing, the one you go to because there is nowhere past Him. He did not father and was not fathered, which rules out any family of gods and any divine lineage. And nothing is comparable to Him, which closes the last door: whatever picture you have formed while reading the first three lines, it is not Him. The surah works by subtraction, clearing away every resemblance until only the claim of oneness is left standing.
units.historicalContext: Several early reports say the surah came in answer to a direct question — describe your Lord to us, tell us what He is made of, tell us His ancestry. The questioners are variously identified in the sources and scholars differ on which account is strongest, but the shape of the reply fits all of them: it refuses the terms of the question rather than answering inside them.

keyTerms.note: Not the ordinary word for the number one. It denies not just plurality but the possibility of being counted alongside anything.

Appears only here in the Quran. Classical commentators offered a range of readings — the one sought in need, the one with no hollow in Him, the one who remains when everything else ends — and generally treated them as complementary rather than rival.
Used of things that can be set side by side and weighed against each other. The line says no such thing exists.
Not a word in the surah, but the name given to what the surah states. The surah is often called Surat al-Tawhid for that reason.

units.lifeInProphetsTime: The Kaaba in the years before the message was surrounded by idols belonging to particular tribes, each with its own story and, often, its own divine family tree. A surah that denies both offspring and ancestry was denying the structure those stories were built on.
units.didYouKnow: A well-known hadith describes this surah as equal to a third of the Quran. Commentators generally explain that the Quran's subject matter falls into law, narrative and belief about God, and that this surah covers the last of the three completely.
units.theologicalSignificance: The surah says what God is not more than what He is, and that restraint is the point. Every positive description risks smuggling in a comparison; the fourth line exists to remove the ones the first three might have left behind.

crossReferences.why: Nothing is like Him — the same denial of comparison, stated directly.
Ayat al-Kursi describes the same self-sufficiency at greater length.
Answers the question of offspring in the same terms.
Warns against setting up comparisons for God.

units.applyIt: Notice, once today, where you have quietly made something else the thing everything depends on — a person's approval, a number in an account, a plan working out. Say the second line and see whether it lands anywhere.
